10065-the-constitution-of-the-united-sta:
James M. Beck, Solicitor-General of the United States and honorary bencher of Gray's Inn, wrote this brief study of the Constitution's genesis, formulation, and political philosophy. A preface by the Earl of Balfour introduces the work, which takes Proverbs as its motto: where there is no vision, the people perish.

Beck traces how the Constitution was made and what ideas shaped it, for readers who want the document's story rather than a lawyer's commentary. His tone is reverent and clear. Students of American government get a compact, early twentieth-century account of the founding charter.
10131-required-poems-for-reading-and-mem:
This school book gathers required poems for reading and memorizing in the third and fourth grades, as prescribed by state courses of study. Its poems are chosen to be learned by heart as well as read aloud, building memory and taste together.

Among them are Robert Louis Stevenson's Autumn Fires, with autumn bonfires in other gardens and all up the vale. Short, musical, and clear, the selections suit young voices. Teachers and parents get a period anthology of what American schoolchildren were expected to know by heart. The poems reward voices that learn them well.
10618-jesus-says-so-or-a-memorial-of-lit:
Published in Boston in 1851 by the Massachusetts Sabbath School Society, this short religious memorial tells the life of a poor London girl called Sarah G. Her father was hurt in an accident early in 1847 and spent weeks in hospital, leaving the family short of food and help. Sarah, quiet and obedient at home, bore the hardship without complaint.

The account follows her faith as she grows, her kindness to her family, and her early death, which revealed a depth of belief others had not seen. Written for Sunday school readers, it holds Sarah up as a model of patience and trust. It also gives a plain window onto poverty, illness, and church life in London in the 1840s.
11760-the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-1:
Compiled by Grenville Kleiser with help from leading preachers, the tenth volume of a 1908 sermon anthology gathers eleven addresses, from Henry Drummond to John Henry Jowett. Each sermon opens with a short biographical note on its preacher, followed by the full text and a general index to preachers and scripture passages.

Drummond's address on love as the greatest thing in the world leads the set. Later sermons take up assurance in God, the Bible against unbelief, and the reconciliation of humanity with God. Read together, they show late Victorian and Edwardian preaching at its most earnest, aimed at ordinary readers rather than scholars alone.
17170-a-study-of-pueblo-pottery-as-illus:
Frank Hamilton Cushing's Bureau of Ethnology study traces Zuni culture growth through pueblo pottery. Chapters show homes shaped by land: round houses to rectangles, flat and terraced roofs from mesa sites, added stories from cliff limits, and communal pueblos from gathered tribes. Pottery follows the same path, from basketry and clay-lined baskets to forms, firing, and decoration.

Figures show hogans, round houses, cliff dwellings, terraced pueblos, and gourd vessels in wicker. Cushing links pots to houses, land, and ritual in a bold, early theory of growth. Students of Southwest peoples will find a classic, richly pictured study of how craft and culture grew together.
17956-recreation-by-viscount-grey-of-fal:
Viscount Grey of Fallodon gave Recreation as an address at the Harvard Union on December 8, 1919, printed in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin in 1920. Grey, a British statesman, asks why an age of plenty seems so full of discontent.

He doubts that ours is a pleasure-finding age, despite films, motor cars, and wealth. He names four things that make for happiness: a moral standard, a good home life, work that justifies life, and true recreation. The address is calm, wise, and short, a classic plea for leisure well used, and still apt for readers who chase fun and miss joy.
17970-the-olden-time-series-vol-1-curios:
Henry M. Brooks made this first volume of the Olden-Time Series from old Boston and Salem newspapers, sources few readers could reach. The series aimed to feed a growing taste for quaint notes of ye olden time, in small, cheap handbooks that were both fun and instructive.

This volume gathers curiosities of the old lottery, when towns and colleges raised funds by chance draws. Later volumes would cover spinning-wheels, strange punishments, quaint ads, and literary oddities. Brooks writes with a light, antiquarian charm. It is a pleasant dip into early New England print, best read in short bites.
18534-the-hurricane-guide-being-an-attem:
William Radcliff Birt wrote this hurricane guide, published by John Murray in London in 1850, publisher to the Admiralty. Birt attempts to connect the rotatory gale with atmospheric waves. He gives instructions for observing waves and storms, with practical directions for avoiding storm centers. A pocket in the book holds two rings of stiff cardboard, to be laid on a chart without breaking the continuity of its lines.

Chapters treat phenomena of revolving storms, phenomena of atmospheric waves, and observations, with instruments, times, localities, seasons, and storms, hurricanes, and typhoons. Practical directions for avoiding storm centers close the guide. Birt writes for seamen of Her Majesty's navy and merchant service, who must watch sky and sea to live. Readers get Victorian storm science in usable form: theory, instruments, and rules for keeping a ship out of a hurricane's heart.
24665-a-soldier-s-life-being-the-persona:
Edwin G. Rundle, late sergeant-major in Her Majesty's Leicestershire Regiment of Foot, wrote these personal reminiscences, published at Toronto in 1909 in an author's edition. Rundle had served as instructor and lecturer to the Military School at Toronto from 1866 to 1868, and he was a member of the Red River Expedition.

Major Henry J. Woodside introduces the book, noting the many recent histories of Britain's imperial wars. Rundle's own story gives the soldier's view from the ranks, with drill, service, and campaign life. Readers of military history will find it a plain, lively memoir of a Victorian non-commissioned officer.
28758-philosophical-transactions-of-the-:
This volume collects the first year of the Royal Society's journal, covering 1665 and 1666, printed in London for the Society's printers. The Philosophical Transactions was the world's first journal devoted to new science, and its early numbers report what learned men were doing across Europe: experiments, instruments, observations, and letters between natural philosophers.

Readers meet science in its first draft form, with short reports rather than finished theories, and a dedication to the Society that frames the whole effort. The old spelling and plain reports give a direct sense of how the scientific community first learned to share results in print. For historians of science, it is a ground-floor record of the Royal Society's founding years.
28823-the-works-of-george-meredith-a-lin:
Edited by David Widger, this linked index covers the Project Gutenberg editions of George Meredith's works. The index gathers Meredith's novels, including The Ordeal of Richard Feverel, Sandra Belloni, and Rhoda Fleming. Evan Harrington, Vittoria, Harry Richmond, Beauchamp's Career, and Diana of the Crossways follow, with full chapter lists for each. His short works and The Shaving of Shagpat appear as well.

The volume is a map rather than a novel: it lets readers find their way through Meredith's long and difficult books, chapter by chapter. Meredith, a leading Victorian novelist, wrote complex prose about love, class, and English society, and this index helps a modern reader plan a path through it. It pairs with the Gutenberg texts to make his whole shelf navigable from one file.
29483-the-little-brown-hen-hears-the-son:
Jasmine Stone Van Dresser wrote this 1908 children's book, printed by Paul Elder and Company of San Francisco and New York, with pictures by William T. Van Dresser. Its heroine, a little brown hen, hears the song of the nightingale and finds a golden harvest. An introduction by Margaret Beecher White frames the tales, and a motto warns that the loudest talkers are not always wisest.

The gander in one tale insists the hen must learn his language, calling her chatter silly and drilling all to say honk. Van Dresser's fables teach listening, humility, and kindness through barnyard talk. Young readers and lovers of old picture books will find a gentle, beautifully made volume of animal tales.
31415-stained-glass-work-a-text-book-for:
C. W. Whall's Stained Glass Work, a text-book for students and workers in glass, belongs to the Artistic Crafts Series of technical handbooks edited by W. R. Lethaby and published by D. Appleton and Company of New York. Whall, with diagrams by two of his apprentices and other illustrations, covers the craft in two parts, from design and glass cutting to glazing, as the frontispiece on cutting and glazing shows. The book is a working manual, not a history.

Whall writes for makers: students learning the trade and workers already at the bench. His instructions are practical, covering materials, tools, leading, and painting on glass. For readers interested in the Arts and Crafts movement, the book shows a master craftsman passing on a medieval art in modern workshop terms, with clarity and pride in good work.
31843-of-six-medi-val-women-to-which-is-:
Alice Kemp-Welch's 1913 book Of Six Mediaeval Women, with a note on mediaeval gardens, published by Macmillan, studies six women across six centuries. They are Roswitha the nun, tenth-century dramatist; Marie de France, twelfth-century romance writer; and Mechthild of Magdeburg, thirteenth-century mystic and Beguine. The others are Mahaut, Countess of Artois, fourteenth-century art patron; Christine de Pisan, fifteenth-century feminist; and Agnes Sorel.

Illustrations include Roswitha presenting her poem to Emperor Otho the First, a lady playing the harp, and a banquet with minstrels. Readers get a pioneering work of women's history, recovering writers, patrons, and mystics whom older histories had passed over.
32595-a-woman-s-wartime-journal-an-accou:
Dolly Sumner Lunt, writing as Mrs. Thomas Burge, kept this diary on her Georgia plantation through the Civil War, here with an introduction and notes by Julian Street. Entries run from January 1864, when prices soar and war still rages, into late 1865.

Lunt records cannon fire near Atlanta, flight on the roads, and frantic efforts to hide mules, meat, and clothes from troops. When Sherman's army passes her house, it tears down fences and cuts a road through her yard, and her plain daily notes show war as a household ordeal.
34299-homo-culture-or-the-improvement-of:
Homo Culture, or the Improvement of Offspring Through Wiser Generation, is a health book by Holbrook, a doctor of physick. He ran a sheet on health and wrote past books on the brain, on memory, and on chastity. This is a new, large form of his past book on the breed of man.

It came out at New York and London from his own house. A front print shows the model baby at eighteen months, the ideal the book would breed toward. Its case, in the terms of its day, is that wise choice in who weds and how they live can lift the health and mind of the young to come. It is a plan book of the breed reform thought of its age.
34501-wolf-and-coyote-trapping-an-up-to-:
Harding wrote this up-to-date wolf hunter's guide, Wolf and Coyote Trapping, printed at Columbus, Ohio, with copyright in 1909. The subtitle promises the best methods of seasoned wolfers for hunting and trapping these animals. Their habits are given in detail as well. A map shows the range of the timber wolf, and pictures show tracks, dens, traps, and catches.

Chapters treat the timber wolf and the coyote first, then the killing of stock and game and the bounties paid. Hunting young wolves, hunting with dogs, and still hunting follow in order. Poisoning, trapping, scents, and baits fill the heart of the book. Blind sets and snow sets close the methods, with rules to remember.
34550-franz-joseph-haydn-the-story-of-th:
Thomas Tapper wrote the Haydn volume in the Child's Own Book of Great Musicians. Theodore Presser at Philadelphia put it out, with rights held in 1917. Its full title calls Haydn the choir boy who became a great composer. A blank page lets the child owner sign the book. Spaces stand for the dates of the composer's birth and death, to be filled.

Joseph Haydn was born in Rohrau, a little Austrian village near Hainburg. The River Leytha flows by it, the tale tells its young readers. Look for the town in any large geography, Tapper urges. The parents lived in a very modest house of one story. A picture of that house is worth studying and remembering, he says. Tapper had written music talks and studies in music biography for children. The book gives a great life in a child's measure.
40338-the-further-adventures-of-mr-verda:
The Further Adventures of Mr Verdant Green, an Oxford undergraduate, is a comic novel by Cuthbert Bede. It continues The Adventures of Mr Verdant Green, an Oxford Freshman. The second edition was printed at London in 1854, with many pictures designed and drawn on the wood by the author himself.

The chapters follow Verdant Green as he starts his Oxford life anew. He does as he has been done by, tries to keep his spirits up, and learns the difference between town and gown. He feathers his oars, eats a dove-tart and a spread-eagle, and spends a merry Christmas. Later he makes his first appearance on any stage, enjoys a real cigar, and gets through his Smalls, the first exam. A second part takes him on as an undergraduate again. The book is a light satire of Oxford ways, full of pranks and scrapes.
40979-a-letter-to-sir-samuel-shepherd-kn:
A Letter to Sir Samuel Shepherd takes up the prosecution of Richard Carlile. Carlile was a printer prosecuted for publishing Paine's Age of Reason. The letter was printed and published by Carlile at 55 Fleet Street. Shepherd was the king's attorney-general, the officer bringing the suit. A society for the suppression of vice joined in the prosecution.

The writer submits remarks on the nature and tendency of the suit. Such prosecutions are not novel, he owns. The accused meets three pleadings to his one allowed plea, he charges. Interruptions from the judge add to that load. That the accuser should plead thrice to the accused's once is flagrant injustice. Though it may be law, it is injustice still, he holds. He meets beforehand the hackneyed arguments he expects in court. The letter pleads free printing against the vice society.
43562-company-g:
Barlow wrote 'Company G,' a record of the services of one company of the 157th New York Volunteers in the War of the Rebellion, published by Hall at Syracuse in 1899. The dates run from September 19, 1862, to July 10, 1865, and the roster of the company is included. The preface says the little work was long contemplated: records of the volunteer organizations sent from Canastota and vicinity should be preserved for the families of the boys.

Barlow claims accuracy in events and dates rather than literary merit, and warns readers about his grammar where he individualizes a collective noun. Commanding officers, he says, have been removed from the high pedestals of war-gods and are considered only as men. The men who fought Company G are called rebels, as the boys knew them, and the book is an offering to comrades from a comrade who marched with them.
44335-curialia-miscellanea-or-anecdotes-:
Curialia Miscellanea is a book of anecdotes of old times by Samuel Pegge, printed in London by Nichols, Son, and Bentley in 1818. Pegge, who died in 1796, was an antiquary and a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries. His portrait, engraved from a painting of 1788, fronts the volume.

The subtitle promises anecdotes that are regal, noble, and miscellaneous. Authentic anecdotes of the royal household appear, with the manners and customs of the court at an early period of English history. Plates show Whittington church, its rectory, and a Revolution house. Pegge's earlier Curialia and his anecdotes of the English language are named on the title page. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
45957-garden-pests-in-new-zealand-a-popu:
Garden Pests in New Zealand is a handbook for growers, farmers, and schools, by a doctor of science at a research house in Nelson. He served that house as its deputy head and its chief student of insects. The book came out as one of a set of tracts from that house.

A note at the front tells how the text was set for print, with old spellings left as they stood in the source. The parts then open with a broad survey of pest kinds and move to the pests of the garden in turn. Its aim is plain use: to name the foe, tell its habits, and guide the man or woman who must fight it in soil and crop.
54530-the-knife-grinder-s-budget-of-pict:
William Walker of Otley printed 'The Knife-Grinder's Budget of Pictures and Poetry, for Boys and Girls' in 1829, priced at one penny, with the knife-grinder himself as frontispiece. Each page pairs a picture with a short rhymed caption. A drill-sergeant cries 'Swing-up, my Lads' on the cover, and the budget opens with an old woman crying her fine apples for eating or pies.

Trade and street figures follow in rhyme. The huxter and his donkey go to market for butter and eggs, the barber is full of news, and a brush-seller cries cheap brushes. Animals carry their own morals: a goat asleep on a crag, and a calf coming for the butcher. A hen calling her chickens teaches children to obey their parents. Sailors fetch silk, cotton, sugar, coffee, and tea across the great sea, and a bull-baiting scene ends the book.
57024-patrins-to-which-is-added-an-inqui:
Patrins is a book of essays by Louise Imogen Guiney, printed at Boston by Copeland and Day in 1897. To it is added an Inquirendo into the wit and other good parts of Charles the Second. Guiney dedicates the volume to Bliss Carman. A patrin, she explains from Romano Lavo-Lil, is a Gypsy trail sign.

A patrin is a handful of leaves or grass cast by the Gypsies on the road, to show those behind the way they have taken. These wild dry whims, she says, are patrins dropped in the open for our tribe. On each she has put its date. One essay begins with a philosopher in Paris for the first time, a dozen years before. Guiney's essays are learned, gay, and combative, on books, kings, and Catholic letters. The little volume is a trail of bright leaves through her reading life.
57383-project-gutenberg-edition-of-the-m:
David Widger compiled a Project Gutenberg edition of the memoirs of four Civil War generals, Grant, Sherman, Sheridan, and Logan. Full tables of contents with links head the set. The Grant memoirs stand first, in two volumes. Grant chapters start with ancestry, birth, and boyhood, then West Point and graduation. Army life and the causes of the Mexican War follow in order.

Grant tale then runs through Corpus Christi, the advance to the Rio Grande, and the battles of Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma. Monterey, Vera Cruz, Cerro Gordo, and the march on Mexico City fill later chapters. The storming of Chapultepec and the peace talks close the Mexican span in volume one. Readers get four famed Union leaders in their own words in one set. The Grant life alone is a landmark of American memoir writing.
57868-the-middle-kingdom-volume-1-of-2-a:
Wells Williams surveys China in The Middle Kingdom, volume one of two, in a revised edition by a Yale professor of Chinese language and literature. His subtitle promises the geography, government, literature, social life, arts, and history of the Chinese empire and its inhabitants. A front illustration shows the emperor kneeling before the shrine of Shangti at the Altar of Heaven.

That plate's caption decodes the ceremony: tablets to imperial ancestors flank the central shrine, with side altars for the sun, the night luminary, all stars, the twenty-eight constellations, and the five elements. Altars also serve the superintendents of snow, rain, wind, and thunder. Williams had written dictionaries of the Chinese language, named on his title page, and the survey rests on long residence and study.
60365-the-collected-writings-of-dougal-g:
The Collected Writings of Dougal Graham, the Skellat bellman of Glasgow, were edited by George MacGregor and printed at Glasgow in 1883 for subscribers and private circulation. The impression was strictly limited to 250 copies; the text here comes from copy number 187. A portrait from the woodcut in the 1774 third edition of Graham's History of the Rebellion fronts the first volume.

MacGregor adds notes, a life of Graham, a bibliography, and a sketch of the chap literature of Scotland. The preface records a debt unpaid: Scott and Motherwell both meant to preserve the pedlar-bellman's works and fame, and neither found the chance. Fifty years on, MacGregor takes up the task, gathering writings that had floated about the country in cheap print, in two volumes.
64219-the-collected-writings-of-dougal-g:
George Mac Gregor edited the Collected Writings of Dougal Graham, the bellman of Glasgow, in two volumes dated eighteen eighty-three. Graham was known by the nickname Skellat. The set was printed for subscribers and private sharing at Glasgow.

Volume two opens with Jockey and Maggy's Courtship, told in five parts. The Coalman's Courtship and the Comical Transactions of Lothian Tom follow. Graham's History of John Cheap the Chapman stands among his best-known chap-book pieces. The editor notes that one piece is reprinted from a rare copy once held by Doctor David Laing. A sketch of the chap literature of Scotland frames the set.
64637-doomsday-257-a-g:
Bryce Walton wrote a science fiction novelet that ran in Planet Stories in May 1952. Cadmus waits on a barren asteroid, in a small dome of lab and living quarters, for the matter transmitter to send him to Mars. Cold pounds at the walls of that small dot of life and warmth.

Venusian scientist Johlan has raised Cadmus and Zaleel for a great plan, and veiled Cadmus' memory against the Silver Guard's mind probers. Zaleel has already gone through the transmitter to her part of the work. Cadmus carries only a sword and a small energy gun against the Great Gray God, a vast machine mind at Akal-jor. Failure, he knows, means the fall of three worlds.
64699-a-history-of-the-comstock-silver-l:
Dan De Quille's history of the Comstock Lode mines Nevada's great silver ground. De Quille was the pen name of William Wright, the title page notes. The work first came out in 1889 and was reprinted in 1974. Its full scope takes in the Great Basin region as well. Lake Tahoe and the high Sierras fall inside that wide frame.

The book sets out the hills, lakes, rivers, and hot springs there. It treats the farm and mineral wealth of what men called Silverland. Towns, camps, mills, and railways of Nevada get their due in it. Great shafts, tunnels, and water works are set out in detail. Lumber flumes and pine woods of the slope round out the survey. The preface starts with the whole state before the parts.
66992-the-law-of-hotel-life-or-the-wrong:
The Law of Hotel Life, or the Wrongs and Rights of Host and Guest is a legal handbook by R Vashon Rogers Jr, a barrister of Osgoode Hall, published in 1879. Rogers wrote it at his publishers' suggestion as a companion to The Wrongs and Rights of a Traveller, gathering the rules that govern inns and their guests.

Chapters define a common inn and innkeeper, then take up city houses, accidents, rooms, and dogs. Later chapters cover guests, wagers and games, safes and baggage, fire, rats, and burglars, and horses and stables. The preface, dated at Kingston, Ontario, in March 1879, concedes that mistakes will be found but hopes the collection serves travellers and hosts alike. It shows how much of daily law once turned on the inn.
67893-the-rover-boys-shipwrecked-or-a-th:
Arthur Winfield wrote The Rover Boys Shipwrecked, for Grosset and Dunlap. Winfield is Edward Stratemeyer under his series pen name. A thrilling hunt for pirates' gold is the subtitle of the tale. A plate shows a boy throwing a hatchet with all his force. Winfield had written the Rover Boys at School to open the line.

The first series runs to twenty titles in the front list. The second series begins with the Rovers at Colby Hall. On snowshoe island, under canvas, and on a hunt follow there. In the land of luck and at big horn ranch stand late in it. Shipwrecked closes the second list as its newest volume. A foreword recalls how the line began with the school book. Stratemeyer gives the Rovers salt water and buried gold.
68412-philosophical-transactions-vol-l-p:
Philosophical Transactions, volume fifty, part two, is one half-year's issue of the Royal Society's journal, covering the year 1758 and printed in 1759. The journal carried the papers read before the society: the undertakings, studies, and labours of the ingenious in many parts of the world, as its title page boasts.

The contents show the range of that world. A letter from Benjamin Franklin reports the effects of electricity in paralytic cases, addressed to John Pringle. Observations of the comet of the autumn of 1757 come from the Hague, sent to the Astronomer Royal. Natural history, medicine, astronomy, and experiment stand side by side, as they did in the society's meetings. The volume is a cross-section of science in the age of reason, when a colonial printer's trials with electricity could share a journal with the King's astronomer.
69847-travels-through-central-africa-to-:
Rene Caillie crossed Africa to Timbuctoo in the years 1824 to 1828, and Colburn and Bentley published his travels at London in 1830. This is the first of two volumes. The advertisement tells why the book mattered. For half a century the existence of a city in the heart of Africa had drawn expeditions, and all had perished or been baffled. Major Laing alone reached the goal, and his papers were lost with his murder.

Caillie, a Frenchman with no resources but his own, reached Timbuctoo and came back alive. The Geographical Society of Paris voted him a premium of 10,000 francs. His road ran east from the Senegal colony by Kakondy, Kankan, and Timbo, then north through a hundred villages to Jenne, and on to the city. From there the title promises the crossing of the desert to Morocco. The English edition made his name across Europe.
70011-travels-through-central-africa-to-:
Rene Caillie wrote Travels Through Central Africa to Timbuctoo, Volume Two. Henry Colburn and Richard Bentley issued it at London in 1830. The journey ran from 1824 to 1828. Caillie crossed the great desert to Morocco as well. A plate list fronts this second volume. His portrait fronts the first.

Maps general and route-wise aid the text. A Timbuctoo woman and the great mosque get plates. Caillie meditates on the Koran in one view. His notes were writ in haste and fear, he says. Strange letters found on him meant death, he knew. Fifteen months passed after his return home. Print waited on that slow work of writing up. A lone Frenchman's disguised trek to a closed city stands among the great feats of African travel.
a-study-of-pueblo-pottery-as-illustrativ: Frank Hamilton Cushing studies Pueblo pottery as a guide to Zuni ways of life, in this paper from the Bureau of Ethnology's fourth annual report. The contents trace homes shaped by their surrounds, square forms from round ones, stepped roofs from sloping mesa sites, and shared pueblos from cliff-house tribes. Pottery follows the same logic. Seen first in basketry and hinted at by clay-lined basketry, it is shaped by its earth, its firing, its form, its paint, and its signs.
doe-osti-2573966-high-performance-solven:
Final technical report DE-FE0032216, from Susteon Inc. under Aravind Rabindran with S. James Zhou, Raghubir P. Gupta, and colleagues, covers January 2023 to January 2025. The goal was a better solvent for stripping carbon dioxide from natural gas combined cycle flue gas. Amine absorption is the mature route, but capture costs run near seventy-two dollars per tonne, and the solvent itself drives much of that cost.

The team synthesized and characterized a promoted solvent, then upgraded a bench-scale test system to screen it. Screening weighed four traits: how much carbon dioxide the solvent holds, how fast it absorbs, how fast it degrades, and the heat needed to release the gas. Formulation work then optimized the blend and down-selected a winner. The targets were lower reboiler energy, faster kinetics, better stability, and smaller environmental impact. A conceptual process design for the full capture plant closes the report.
doe-osti-3000013-lower-snake-river-dams-:
Pavel Etingov, Sohom Datta, Slaven Kincic and co-workers at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory weigh what four big dams give the power grid, in PNNL-38452, dated September 2025. The Lower Snake River dams in Washington generate hydroelectric power for the Bonneville Power Administration. Debate over the dams often counts only their energy. This study counts their grid services too, the quiet jobs that keep the western power system stable second by second.

Using public data, the team scored energy capacity, supply balancing, ramping speed, voltage and reactive power support, frequency response and transmission effects. The plants performed as expected for their size. Their balancing, ramping and reserve contributions mattered most at peak load and during weather events. Frequency and voltage support were measurable as well. Appendices chart five years of regional generation and load, 2020 to 2024, so the service claims rest on visible operating history.
doe-osti-3000792-second-generation-non-a:
Jak Tanthana of RTI International leads this final report on second-generation non-aqueous solvents for carbon capture, covering April 2023 to March 2025. Gas-fired power plants vent dilute carbon dioxide that standard water-based amine scrubbers capture only at high energy cost. A water-lean solvent should strip the gas with less heat wasted on boiling water, and this project carried one candidate family, GEN2NAS, from flask to bench plant.

Laboratory testing measured how the solvent absorbs and releases carbon dioxide, and kinetic studies timed those reactions. About 50 litres of solvent were then made and loaded into RTI's bench-scale gas absorption system, a small absorber-regenerator loop modelled on the traditional amine process. That familiarity is a selling point for plant operators. Process simulation and a techno-economic assessment close the report, pricing the system for a full natural gas combined cycle plant.
doe-osti-3018250-communications-reliabil:
Pranav Gadamsetty and Dhananjay Anand wrote this February 2026 report, NLR/TP-5400-95681, on communications reliability for vehicle grid integration. As utilities steer electric vehicle charging, the messages between vehicles, chargers, and grid software become part of the power system. If those messages fail silently, charging sessions fail with them. The report works through use cases one by one.

Early cases cover telematics-based scheduled charging and day-ahead pricing optimization. Each case maps the communications architecture, draws the message sequence, and runs a reliability analysis. Failure tables get specific: one entry tracks a system reporting the wrong active charge session when meter values cannot be decoded, with hundreds of affected sessions counted in the analysis data. Distributed energy management systems sit at the receiving end of much of this traffic. Grid software teams get a reliability checklist written from real failure modes, not theory.
doe-osti-3020301-em-porin-inspired-ionom:
Shudipto Konika Dishari's final report for a DOE Early Career project describes a new family of ion-conducting polymers modeled on the ion channels of living cells. The polymers, called ionomers, carry ring-shaped calix[4]arene units that form pores smaller than a nanometer. The aim was molecular-level control over how fast ions move through membranes and how selective that movement is, with fuel cells as the target application.

The team synthesized the macrocyclic ionomers and traced proton movement through them, using nuclear magnetic resonance to measure water diffusion in films about 300 nanometers thick at full humidity. The sub-nanometer pores sped ion transport and, under an applied field, behaved like ionic diodes that pass current one way. The report draws design rules for membranes and catalyst binders in proton exchange membrane fuel cells.
doe-osti-3362555-key-performance-indicat:
Casey W. Quinn, Dhananjay Anand, and Nadia Panossian set out scorecards for vehicle grid integration in this report, first published December 31, 2024 and revised September 12, 2025. Electric cars could help the grid by charging at smart times, but utilities need shared yardsticks to prove it. The report defines key performance indicators in five families: reliability, responsiveness, participation, energy, and interoperability, each with a formula and an owner.

Sample measures show the flavor. Availability counts the seconds a car sits plugged in and free for smart charging. A flexibility score counts how long a charge could have waited without hurting the driver. One responsiveness metric divides the schedule shift, in kilowatt-hours, by the incentive dollars paid. The closing section lays out next steps for programs that adopt the set.
doe-osti-3363716-resstock-measure-docume:
Katelyn Stenger, Lixi Liu, Philip White, and four colleagues at the National Laboratory of the Rockies document a ResStock measure (NLR/TP-5500-96634, May 2026). The measure installs a high efficiency natural gas furnace across modeled homes. The furnace is rated at 95 percent AFUE. It is one volume in the ResStock 2025 Release 1 documentation series.

The upgrade logic is universal: every household with existing ductwork receives the gas furnace, whatever its original fuel. The report explains how building characteristics translate into OpenStudio-HPXML parameters, where baseline assumptions enter, and how to access the modeled results. Analysts use such measures to compare heating pathways consistently across the national housing stock.
doe-osti-3364915-resstock-measure-docume:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5500-96827, by Lixi Liu, Jeff Maguire, and Yingli Lou, documents the natural gas water heater measure for ResStock 2025 Release 1. ResStock simulates the national housing stock, and this measure models replacing water heaters with natural gas units, both storage tank and tankless designs. The document fixes every input so other analysts can reproduce the runs.

Tables list the arguments ResStock passes to OpenStudio-HPXML, flagging which values the simulation calculates itself. The high-efficiency condensing tankless case carries a uniform energy factor of 0.98. Defaults cover tank volume, recovery efficiency, standby loss, and backup heating capacity. As with its companion volumes, the value lies in transparency: anyone auditing the national model can trace exactly what a gas water heater upgrade assumes.
doe-osti-3375449-multi-material-hydrodyn:
Los Alamos National Laboratory slide set LA-UR-26-25234, by Eduardo Lozano of the Theoretical Division, teaches multi-material flow simulation with the Ghost Fluid Method. The slides were made for the LANL Co-Design Summer School, held June 11, 2026. Flows with more than one material show up in impacts, sprays, and explosions. Each material obeys its own equation of state. The hard part is the seam where two materials meet.

Lozano starts with terms: material, phase, and species are kept apart. A glass of soda with ice and gas makes the point in plain form. The Ghost Fluid Method then fills fake cells past each seam. Those ghost states let a solver treat each side as if the other were more of itself. Filling them takes extrapolation, and the slides weigh two styles. One marches a time-like equation outward. The other solves a static equation with fast sweeping.
doe-osti-3380282-recycle-ga-from-e-waste:
Recycle Ga from E-Waste Containing GaN/GaAs Chips is a CRADA final report, NLR/TP-6A20-99424 from July 2026, written under an American-Made E-Scrap Prize voucher. The agreement number is CRD-25-31747, and Tapajyoti Ghosh is the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact and cited author. Funding came from the Advanced Manufacturing and Materials Technologies Office.

Gallium is a critical material for semiconductors, and it sits inside discarded gallium nitride and gallium arsenide chips in the e-waste stream. The prize voucher mechanism pairs a winning recycler with laboratory expertise; here the work targeted recovering gallium from those chips rather than mining new supply. The report closes the voucher project and records what the laboratory contributed to the recycling process.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAFassnachtGeo:
George E. Fassnacht had worked for the CIA, and by January 1975 he was in court trying to get his arsenal back. Dave Racher reported for the Philadelphia Daily News on January 20 that Fassnacht had lost his bid to recover what the government had seized.

The seized stock was not a hunter's cabinet: machine guns, explosives, and 363,000 rounds of ammunition. Cases like his fed the era's fascination with former intelligence men and their private arsenals after Watergate. The single article is preserved as a newspaper record of the judgment and the strange inventory behind it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GarrisonJimDoJG: Floyd D. Moore of the Internal Revenue Service swore an affidavit in June 1971 in support of a complaint and search warrants. The filing belongs to the federal government's case touching New Orleans District Attorney Jim Garrison, whose name heads the archive file. The surviving record gives the agent, his agency, and the month, but not the affidavit's charges in detail.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LatinAmericaGen: Charles Keeley of United Press International wrote 'South America: Armies in Command,' a wire-service survey of the continent's military governments. The piece belongs to the era when generals ruled much of South America and wire reporters summed up the pattern for American readers. The file gives the title, the author, and the subject, but no date and no further detail about which countries the survey covered or what it concluded.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LawsonWinstonG_:
A researcher compiled these notes on the official statement of Winston Lawson, a Secret Service agent who worked on the Dallas motorcade. The notes run to five pages on Lawson's account. They take up the Air Force One passenger manifest, the first shot as the motorcade passed under the overpass, and the emergency-room response at the hospital.

Lawson's statement formed part of the record the Warren Commission relied on. A private researcher's notes show the other side of that record: readers outside government checking each claim against the rest of the file. The notes record what one close reader found important in Lawson's words, and what he found doubtful.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NorthrupWilliam:
On January 25, 1968, the office of Senator Robert F. Kennedy answered a mailing from William G. Northrup. Northrup had sent his booklet, 'The Overlooked Factor, Or — A Rendezvous With Death!' The senator's office acknowledged receiving it, in the form letter such mailings drew.

Citizens mailed theories to senators by the sackful in those years, and Kennedy's office received more than most. Four months later, Kennedy himself was assassinated. A polite acknowledgment is thin evidence of anything but receipt. Still, the letter preserves the traffic: a self-published booklet with a dramatic title, sent to a senator, logged and answered by staff while the events it worried about were still unfolding.
jesus-says-so-or-a-memorial-of-little-sa:
Jesus Says So, a memorial of little Sarah G----, was printed at Boston in 1851 from a London edition. Sarah lived with her parents in a narrow lane in London. Her father was hurt early in 1847 and lay many weeks in hospital. The children often went till afternoon without food, the memorial says, yet Sarah never complained.

Sarah comforts her crying mother with the sparrows text in her last days. God cares for the sparrows, and are not you better than a sparrow, she asks. Pray, and then you will be so happy, she urges. The Sabbath School Society issued the child's story.
nasa-tm-19660026439-solar-evolution-with:
D. Ezer and A. G. W. Cameron, at the Institute for Space Studies in New York, ask a bold question in this paper. What if gravity itself has slowly changed over time? They test that idea, called varying-G cosmology, by recalculating how the Sun evolved under it.

Their model sequence extends their earlier work on early solar evolution. In the varying-G Sun, they find, lithium is used up less than in a constant-G Sun. The time to burn out the central hydrogen also shrinks, helped by much greater helium production. Their present-day model predicts a far higher neutrino output, a claim they note can be checked by experiment.
nasa-tm-19670009029-calculation-of-densi:
V. A. J. van Lint, Felix E. Geiger Jr., and D. K. Nichols describe a calculation method in this paper. Gamma rays passing through a material knock electrons loose, and those electrons damage the material's crystal structure. The authors show how to calculate the density of such defects to be expected.

Their method uses measured rates at which defects appear. It also uses the range-energy curve for electrons and the theoretical spectrum of Compton electrons. They work a specific case: silicon exposed to cobalt-60 gamma rays. Their result agrees reasonably with experimental data, and it corrects an earlier theoretical calculation.
nasa-tm-19680001779-compression-of-the-p:
H. A. Taylor Jr., H. C. Brinton, and M. W. Pharo III, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in November 1967. It studies the compression of the plasmasphere during geomagnetically disturbed periods. The plasmasphere is the fat torus of cold plasma co-rotating around Earth, and magnetic storms squeeze it inward.

Positive ion mass spectrometers aboard the OGO I and OGO III satellites measured hydrogen and helium ions directly during 1965 and 1966. Inside the plasmasphere, ion concentration fell gradually with height, but at the outer boundary, the plasmapause, it dropped abruptly. Sometimes it fell tenfold within a few hundred kilometers. That boundary moved inward and outward in step with planetary magnetic activity, showing large-scale expansion and contraction. During one stormy stretch in July 1966, the boundary was caught unusually low over the nightside Earth.
nasa-tm-19710015486-cosmic-antimatter-an:
F. W. Stecker, D. L. Morgan, and J. Bredekamp of the Goddard Space Flight Center issued this preprint in April 1971, numbered X-641-71-150. It asks whether antimatter exists on a large scale in the universe. When matter meets antimatter, both are destroyed and gamma rays result, so a cosmic gamma-ray glow could betray hidden antimatter.

The authors present early results from a detailed calculation of the gamma-ray spectrum that such annihilation would produce across the cosmos. Their calculated spectrum closely resembles the observed background above one million electron volts. They read that match as possible evidence for large-scale antimatter. The calculation folds in annihilation cross sections, absorption by the intergalactic medium, and photon scattering at high redshifts.
nasa-tm-19710025480-note-on-the-characte:
Kunitomo Sakurai wrote this note in July 1971, numbered X-693-71-267, on the sunspot groups that produce solar proton flares. Sakurai was a NASA associate with the University of Maryland. Most sunspot groups stay quiet, but a few erupt and spray high-energy protons into space, endangering astronauts and spacecraft.

The note argues that the production of solar cosmic rays grows as the gradient, the steepness, of a group's magnetic field increases. Such steep gradients form along with the rotating motion of sunspot groups. Groups whose polarity pattern is reversed prove especially effective at producing proton flares. Sakurai builds on Severny's work, which sorted proton flares into four classes tied to the magnetic field gradient.
podcast-dannyjones-uPTYwIEWH-g:
Shane Lee of the Deck Hands crew sits with Danny Jones for KONCRETE number 8. The session starts in chaos over headphones and gear. Lee would rather skip the fancy setup entirely.

Once settled, the talk turns to boats, work, and the crew's rough humor. Lee tells tales from life on the water near Florida. The tape keeps false starts and swearing in place. That rawness is the point of the early KONCRETE shows. The episode preserves a deckhand's voice before polish, fame, or sponsors smoothed anything out. Lee never tries to sound polished or grand.
podcast-joerogan-2k8xnF1tg-g:
Comedian Dave Landau joins Joe Rogan for episode 2373. Landau is known for dark jokes and a dry delivery. He has drawn praise as a sharp stand-up in the style of past greats.

Early talk turns to Detroit and how the city fell and rose. Landau notes it was once among the richest cities on earth. The pair trade stories about clubs, crowds, and hard years on the road. The episode mixes city history with shop talk from two men who have spent their lives on stage and behind microphones.
podcast-joerogan-6DQSIzJ9J-g:
Do the beings people meet on DMT count as real? Rogan takes up the famous question in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Users of the drug often report meeting playful entities, sometimes called elves, and many insist the beings felt more real than waking life.

Rogan turns the reports over from every side: brain chemistry, shared hallucination, or a door to somewhere else. He draws on his own long interest in the drug and the stories guests have told him. The segment cannot settle the matter, but it states the puzzle well, in the words of a host who has chased it for years.
podcast-joerogan-Lb_1d68vx-g:
Bob Lazar returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2479, this time with Luigi Vendittelli beside him. Lazar's 1989 claims about working on alien craft near Area 51 made him the most famous whistleblower in UFO culture. His first Rogan visit was a landmark for the show.

The talk revisits his story with years of new attention layered on top, including fresh claims and fresh scrutiny. Rogan asks what has changed and what Lazar still cannot prove. For followers of the case, the episode is the latest full statement from a man whose account has been argued over for decades.
podcast-joerogan-m7Hrq8WL1-g:
Warren Smith talks with Rogan for episode 2261 of the Joe Rogan Experience, in a long and open conversation. The entry keeps the full talk as aired, with the guest across hours in the show's standard unscripted form.

The transcript holds the whole back-and-forth, so readers meet the guest's stories and views whole rather than trimmed. Full sittings like this one are the show's basic record, and the library keeps them complete. The episode is filed for listeners and fans who want the entire appearance on file, from the first exchange to the last.
podcast-joerogan-pVbygFFBJ_g:
Joe Rogan roams through brain implants, Iron Man suits, and robot children in a segment from his show. The three topics share one theme: the merge of man and machine. Rogan hosts the tour of what labs now build.

Rogan works through chips that let minds move cursors, suits that grant huge strength, and bots raised to seem like kids. He asks where the line of the human sits as the merge grows. The segment is short and full of awe and doubt. Listeners get a brisk tour of the cyborg age. The library holds the file as an archive record.
podcast-tuckercarlson-rsSmQEJyO-g:
Tucker Carlson reports that the global war on Christians has grown worse and names Senator Ted Cruz as a man who does not care. The episode title makes both the charge and the call-out. Carlson speaks in his own voice.

Carlson lays out fresh cases of Christians jailed, killed, or driven from their homes across the world. He argues US leaders shrug while faith dies abroad. He singles out Cruz for praise of Israel while Christians there suffer, as Carlson sees it. Listeners get the full charge in one place. The library keeps it as a record of his stated view.
recreation-by-viscount-grey-of-fallodon-:
Viscount Grey of Fallodon, K.G., spoke on recreation at the Harvard Union on December 8, 1919, and Houghton Mifflin printed the address in 1920. He doubts at the start that his is a pleasure-finding age, for all its wealth and new amusements. Moving pictures and motor-cars abound, yet content seems scarce and discontent grows.

Grey asks what makes people happy and what they can do to make themselves so. Recreation is one part of happiness, not the chief part, he grants. He names a moral standard to guide one's acts as the first of four other things in our own control, with good home life next.
required-poems-for-reading-and-memorizin:
State courses of study prescribed these poems for reading and memorizing in the third and fourth grades. The set opens with poems by Robert Louis Stevenson. Autumn Fires comes first, picturing bonfires in the gardens and up the vale, their grey smoke towering as summer ends.

Its refrain bids children sing a song of seasons, finding something bright in all. The Unseen Playmate follows, about the Friend of the Children who comes out of the wood when children play alone. No one hears or sees him, the poem says, yet he sings when a child tinkles a musical glass. Later poets in the set fall beyond the pages shown.
the-constitution-of-the-united-states-a-: James M. Beck was solicitor-general of the United States and an honorary bencher of Gray's Inn. He wrote this brief study of the birth, framing, and guiding ideas of the United States Constitution. The Earl of Balfour supplies a preface. Beck dedicates the book to Attorney-General Harry M. Daugherty, dated from Chamonix on July 14, 1922. Balfour's preface recalls Beck's wartime writing for the Allied cause. Only the front matter and the start of that preface are present here.
the-hurricane-guide-being-an-attempt-to-:
William Radcliff Birt published this guide with John Murray of London in 1850. Murray was publisher to the Admiralty. The full title states the project plainly. It connects the rotatory gale with atmospheric waves. It gives instructions for observing both. Practical directions help sailors avoid storm centers. The preface states his aim clearly. He wants to show a link between two phenomena. One is among the most terrific on the globe. The other is little known but closely bound to storms.

Birt leaves the argument's success to the public. His second aim is plain enough. Seamen should learn the essential facts of storms. A mid-century sailor had no forecasts. Reading wave and weather signs could save his ship. It could decide whether he skirted a hurricane or sailed into its center. The book turns storm science into working rules.
the-olden-time-series-vol-1-curiosities-: Curiosities of the Old Lottery is volume 1 of the Olden Time Series, small handbooks prepared by Henry M. Brooks and sold by Ticknor and Company of Boston at 50 cents. Only the publisher's series pages and the title page are present here, so the lottery pieces themselves do not appear. The same series pages open the other Olden Time volumes in this group. Brooks gathered his material chiefly from old Boston and Salem newspapers, and a Salem Gazette notice praises his collecting.
the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-10-drum: The final volume of The World's Great Sermons, compiled by Grenville Kleiser in 1908, is represented by its contents list. Henry Drummond leads with The Greatest Thing in the World. A general index to the ten volumes is included. Other preachers named include Gordon, Dawson, and Gunsaulus. Hillis contributes God the Unwearied Guide. The sermons themselves do not appear in the pages present here.
